items.stem: In March 2022 a deepfake video appeared to show which leader telling soldiers to surrender?
items.answer: Volodymyr Zelenskyy
items.markingKey: Volodymyr Zelenskyy. It was quickly debunked and removed by platforms.

items.stem: Explain why the distinction between misinformation and disinformation matters for interventions.
items.answer: Disinformation involves intent and often coordinated actors, so responses include investigating networks and sanctions; misinformation is shared innocently, so education, labels and friction may be more appropriate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Disinformation involves intent and often coordinated actors, so responses include investigating networks and sanctions; misinformation is shared innocently, so education, labels and friction may be more appropriate. items.stem: Isabel writes: "Only uneducated people believe misinformation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Belief depends on identity, emotion, trust and repetition; highly educated people also share misinformation that fits their views (motivated reasoning).
items.markingKey: Belief depends on identity, emotion, trust and repetition; highly educated people also share misinformation that fits their views (motivated reasoning). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A deepfake video is first shared by 20 accounts. Each new sharer leads, on average, to 1.5 further shares in the next hour. Estimate the number of new shares in hour 5.
items.answer: about 152

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Falsehood diffused significantly farther, faster, deeper, and more broadly than the truth in all categories of information."
— Vosoughi, Roy and Aral, "The spread of true and false news online", Science, 2018

With reference to the source, explain one implication for platforms.
items.answer: Because false news naturally spreads faster, platforms that optimise for engagement will tend to amplify it unless they add friction, labels or ranking changes.
items.markingKey: Because false news naturally spreads faster, platforms that optimise for engagement will tend to amplify it unless they add friction, labels or ranking changes. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using the Arup deepfake fraud (2024) as an example, explain deepfakes and trust in communication.
items.answer: An employee in Arup's Hong Kong office joined a video call with what appeared to be the CFO and colleagues – all deepfakes – and transferred about US$25 million to fraudsters. Realistic synthetic video defeated normal verification, showing that seeing and hearing are no longer proof of identity.
items.markingKey: Context (An employee in Arup's Hong Kong office joined a video call with what appeared to be the CFO and colleagues – all deepfakes – and transferred about US$25 million to fraudsters.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: realistic synthetic video defeated normal verification, showing that seeing and hearing are no longer proof of identity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to deepfakes and trust in communication.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Misinformation is mainly a problem caused by technology."
items.answer: Technology amplifies and accelerates misinformation, but its causes are social and political as well as technical.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: algorithms amplify engaging falsehoods; cheap tools make fakes easy. Arguments against: rumours and propaganda long predate the internet; demand side: polarisation, low trust and identity; political actors deliberately spread it. Supported judgement: Technology amplifies and accelerates misinformation, but its causes are social and political as well as technical.

items.stem: Explain why disinformation spreads effectively on social media.
items.answer: It is designed to be emotional, novel and identity-affirming, which drives engagement; recommendation algorithms amplify engaging content, sharing is instant, and corrections spread more slowly.

items.stem: Briefly explain why deepfakes create a "liar's dividend".
items.answer: When people know realistic fakes are possible, those caught on genuine recordings can claim the evidence is fake, so deepfakes undermine trust in all audio-visual evidence, not just in the fakes.

items.answer: Misinformation is false information shared without intent to deceive (e.g. a relative forwarding a fake cure); disinformation is deliberately created or spread to deceive (e.g. state-run troll campaigns).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "media literacy"?
options: The process by which platforms review, remove, restrict or label user content according to their rules and the law
The ability to access, analyse, evaluate, create and act using all forms of media
A system in which users or authorities notify a platform of illegal content and the platform must act on it

items.markingKey: B. "media literacy" is the ability to access, analyse, evaluate, create and act using all forms of media.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "content moderation".
items.answer: The process by which platforms review, remove, restrict or label user content according to their rules and the law
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the process by which platforms review, remove, restrict or label user content according to their rules and the law. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which country has repeatedly ranked first in the European Media Literacy Index?
items.answer: Finland
items.markingKey: Finland. Finland teaches media literacy across its curriculum.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a cheapfake and a deepfake.
items.answer: A deepfake is created with AI to synthesise realistic fake media; a cheapfake uses simple editing (slowing, cropping, mislabelling) – e.g. the 2019 slowed-down video of Nancy Pelosi.
items.markingKey: A deepfake is created with AI to synthesise realistic fake media; a cheapfake uses simple editing (slowing, cropping, mislabelling) – e.g. the 2019 slowed-down video of Nancy Pelosi. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "AI can now moderate content perfectly without humans." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: AI misses context, sarcasm and new forms of harm, performs worse in less-resourced languages, and needs human review and appeals.
items.markingKey: AI misses context, sarcasm and new forms of harm, performs worse in less-resourced languages, and needs human review and appeals. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why lateral reading is more effective than reading a website closely.
items.answer: Misleading sites can look professional and cite sources; checking what independent sources say about the publisher and claim quickly reveals bias or falsehood, as Stanford research on fact-checkers showed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Misleading sites can look professional and cite sources; checking what independent sources say about the publisher and claim quickly reveals bias or falsehood, as Stanford research on fact-checkers showed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between automated moderation and human moderation.
items.answer: Automated moderation uses algorithms (hash-matching, classifiers) to handle volume quickly but misses context; human moderation understands nuance but is slow, costly and harmful to moderators' mental health.
items.markingKey: Automated moderation uses algorithms (hash-matching, classifiers) to handle volume quickly but misses context; human moderation understands nuance but is slow, costly and harmful to moderators' mental health. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between fact-checking and media literacy.
items.answer: Fact-checking is professionals verifying specific claims; media literacy is the general set of skills that lets individuals analyse and evaluate media themselves.
items.markingKey: Fact-checking is professionals verifying specific claims; media literacy is the general set of skills that lets individuals analyse and evaluate media themselves. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In a study on a short-video platform, a true news story was reshared 2,400 times on average, while a false story was reshared 4,800 times. Calculate how many percent more the false story was reshared.
items.answer: 100% more

items.stem: A platform's transparency report states it removed 5,000,000 pieces of content for hate speech in a quarter. 8% of removals were appealed and 30% of appeals led to the content being restored. Calculate the number of items restored and the restored items as a percentage of all removals.
items.answer: 120,000 restored; 2.4% of removals
items.markingKey: Appeals = 5,000,000 × 8% = 400,000 [M1]; restored = 400,000 × 30% = 120,000 [A1]; 120,000 ÷ 5,000,000 × 100 = 2.4% [A1]. (This is a minimum estimate of wrongful removals, because most users do not appeal.)

items.stem: Briefly describe Finland's media-literacy education and explain what it reveals about education as an intervention against misinformation.
items.answer: Finland integrated media literacy into its national curriculum and public campaigns after Russian disinformation efforts following 2014; it ranks top in the European Media Literacy Index. A whole-society approach builds long-term resilience rather than relying on removing content.
items.markingKey: Context (Finland integrated media literacy into its national curriculum and public campaigns after Russian disinformation efforts following 2014; it ranks top in the European Media Literacy Index.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a whole-society approach builds long-term resilience rather than relying on removing content. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to education as an intervention against misinformation.

items.stem: With reference to COVID-19 "infodemic", explain how it illustrates the impact of misinformation on health.
items.answer: During the pandemic false claims about cures, vaccines and 5G spread widely; the WHO launched campaigns and platforms added labels and removed some content. False information contributed to vaccine hesitancy and harmful behaviour, showing that misinformation has real health consequences.
items.markingKey: Context (During the pandemic false claims about cures, vaccines and 5G spread widely; the WHO launched campaigns and platforms added labels and removed some content.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: false information contributed to vaccine hesitancy and harmful behaviour, showing that misinformation has real health consequences. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the impact of misinformation on health.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Very large online platforms shall diligently identify, analyse and assess any systemic risks in the Union stemming from the design or functioning of their service."
— EU Digital Services Act, Article 34

Explain how this source shows a change in how platforms are regulated.
items.answer: It moves from regulating individual posts to requiring platforms to assess the risks created by their design and systems (e.g. algorithms), making them responsible for structural harms.
items.markingKey: It moves from regulating individual posts to requiring platforms to assess the risks created by their design and systems (e.g. algorithms), making them responsible for structural harms. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: "Only uneducated people believe misinformation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Belief depends on identity, emotion, trust and repetition; highly educated people also share misinformation that fits their views (motivated reasoning).
items.markingKey: Belief depends on identity, emotion, trust and repetition; highly educated people also share misinformation that fits their views (motivated reasoning). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Governments, rather than platforms, should decide what content is removed online."
items.answer: Democratic laws should define illegal content and oversight (as in the DSA), but day-to-day moderation must be done by platforms under transparency and appeal rules.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: democratic legitimacy and legal accountability; platforms have commercial interests. Arguments against: governments may censor critics (internet shutdowns, blocking); laws differ between countries; speed and scale require platform systems. Supported judgement: Democratic laws should define illegal content and oversight (as in the DSA), but day-to-day moderation must be done by platforms under transparency and appeal rules.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that community-based fact-checking such as Community Notes is better than professional fact-checking.
items.answer: Community notes are a useful complement but slower and less expert; they cannot replace professional fact-checking.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: scales to many posts and is seen as less biased; notes appear only when people with differing views agree. Arguments against: slow; many misleading posts never get notes; less expertise on complex topics; can be manipulated. Supported judgement: Community notes are a useful complement but slower and less expert; they cannot replace professional fact-checking. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "Deepfakes are the greatest threat to democratic elections." Discuss.
items.answer: Deepfakes are a serious and growing threat, but so far they are one of several, and not clearly the greatest, threat to elections.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: realistic fakes can damage candidates days before votes (Slovakia 2023, Biden robocall 2024); liar's dividend undermines trust. Arguments against: research on 2024 elections found limited measurable effect of AI fakes; cheapfakes, targeted ads and mass misinformation are more common; voter suppression and polarisation also threaten elections. Supported judgement: Deepfakes are a serious and growing threat, but so far they are one of several, and not clearly the greatest, threat to elections. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that the Digital Services Act will make social media safer.
items.answer: The DSA can improve safety and accountability, but its effect depends on vigorous enforcement and protection of free expression.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: binding duties, audits and large fines; researcher data access and transparency. Arguments against: enforcement is slow and contested; platforms may comply minimally; risk of over-removal of lawful speech. Supported judgement: The DSA can improve safety and accountability, but its effect depends on vigorous enforcement and protection of free expression. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation.
